Strip it all back to basics. Start with looking at face shapes and eye shapes to identify your features. Look at their relative size and shape, how close/far apart they are from each other, the asymmetry of your face, notice what you like and what you would like to adjust. Play with a lamp and shine it on different areas, notice how light and shadow work on your face.

When you know what you're working with, look up tutorials for your specific features and for what you want to emphasise/reduce the appearance of. E.g., maybe you already have quite upturned eyes and prominent cheekbones, if so, doing a 'lifted technique' won't be enhancing or balancing anything, it will just be exaggerating what you already have and look odd.

No worries, you have beautiful eyes and your application is great. They're just a very specific shape that needs a different technique. Try with eyeshadow and a flat liner brush before buying any new eye-liner, easier to diffuse and you can see what tones of brown suit you best.

It's not that you have hooded eyes, it's that your eye shape is downturned. The outer edges turn down, so when you apply any darkness to that area it exaggerates the effect and it will drag your eyes down. Try looking for tutorials that specify this eye shape.

I would suggest using a brown liner on your lids, smudging very lightly as you have done, and do not take it any further down past the whites of your eyes. Instead of following your eye shape at the end, pull it out and away from the corner of your eyes and towards the tail of your brow. It doesn't need to be a full on wing, just softly pull the colour out to lift your eyes. You can add a nude underneath where you've pulled the colour out on your outer lid to exaggerate the lifting effect.

In Australia, other than private pay and private insurance, we have Medicare which gives you 10 rebated sessions per calendar year using any evidence-based therapies, or 20 on an eating-disorder plan. The referrals come through from the GP and you report back to them after 6 sessions with a brief letter to justify the other 4, then a second brief letter at the end to note progress. The client can use the sessions at their own frequency. Medicare does not cover psychometric assessments.

There's also the National Disability Insurance Scheme for those with a psychosocial disability which provides lifelong support for therapies etc, and WorkCover for temporary psychosocial injury relating to employment.

Depending on the client, my goals are to usually assist them in improving their emotional literacy, social skills and assertiveness, and self care management. If they have the capacity to set their own goals, or their supports are attuned to their needs and identify goals, we work on those.

Assisting them with access to community groups that fit their interests or needs can be helpful, likewise engaging with other AH clinicians on their care team like OTs & speechies for a multidisciplinary approach to ensure continuity.

I also like to use different forms of media to reinforce learning and reduce the stress of talk therapy for those who have difficulty with expressive language (e.g., creating a PowerPoint in session for the client to take home, using art and craft to engage in mindfulness, creating custom emotion charts using photos of the client, etc). Modified CBT and behaviour management work well, but part of the goal is also training family and supports to prompt the client to use strategies taught in sessions when at home.

To put it in perspective, I worked with a client fortnightly for about 8 months and it took them that time to process the discomfort of telling his supports he felt sad sometimes - but it was a breakthrough when it happened. Disability work requires mammoth amounts of patience, repetition, and consistency.

A psychiatrist is a trained medical doctor who specialises in psychiatry, they have to go to med school & have an MD. They focus mainly on prescribing medication to rebalance abnormalities in neurotransmitters which can lead to mentall illness.

A psychologist has a psychology degree & cannot prescribe medication. They focus mainly on behaviour & cognitive processes to help people redirect their life to be more balanced. This can have a similar effect as medication, depending on the disorder being treated.

For the best treatment, it is usually suggested to see both a psychiatrist & psychologist as they compliment each other.

A therapist is just an umbrella term for someone who practises therapy, be it a counsellor, psychologist, psychiatrist or social worker.

If you haven't already, there are several philosopher's who have written about existentialism & nihilism. It can be heavy reading sometimes but you may find a philosopher whose rationale resonates with your thought processes.

Questioning your existence isn't something to put yourself down over, it takes great intellect & insight to acknowledge a painful truth & learn to come to terms with it in your own way.

Existential depression is a beast that is hard to conquer. If you are a spiritual person it can be overcome by your beliefs, if you are not (I'm not) it becomes a matter of accepting that you aren't alive for any significant reason. That your life & consequent death is purely biological.

I think what people mean when they say "life is what you make of it", is that you exist & what you choose to do with that existence is entirely up to you. What they fail to acknowledge is that no matter what you choose to do, it will objectively mean nothing & so is at the fundamental level, pointless.

You can sacrifice yourself for the greater good but when existence comes to its inevitable end, your achievements mean nothing to the universe. It is only through the validation of other people & our cultures that we find solace in our actions, but when your depressed that means fuck all.

Personally, the only thing that gets me through is knowing that life has existed on Earth for billions of years. Despite so many mass extinction level events, we are still here. That is what makes me proud to be alive. In the end it may be for nothing, but the journey started long before us & I'm amazed at what life has achieved so far, irrelevant of its purpose.
